claims.text: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 exhibits a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure operation.
The unmodified alloy has poor mechanical integrity and is prone to cracking.
Mechanical alloying followed by pressureless sintering will produce a homogeneous dispersion of approximately 5 vol% TiC nanoparticles in the alloy matrix.
Dispersed TiC nanoparticles will deflect or arrest cracks.
Dispersed TiC nanoparticles will impede dislocation motion.
The TiC addition will refine the alloy microstructure.
The TiC dispersion will distribute mechanical stress more evenly.
TiC will strengthen and toughen the material through dispersion strengthening and load sharing.
TiC is inert with respect to the phase transition responsible for the alloy's caloric effect.
Approximately 5 vol% TiC will increase compressive strength relative to the pristine alloy.
Approximately 5 vol% TiC will reduce cracking or crack propagation relative to the pristine alloy.
The TiC-reinforced material will retain a caloric response similar in magnitude to that of the pristine alloy.
Keeping the ceramic volume fraction sufficiently low will avoid consequential dilution of the calorically active phase.
TiC reinforcement may cause minor shifts in phase-transition temperature or kinetics.

contradictions.description: The intervention describes adding pre-existing TiC nanoparticles, whereas the hypothesis calls TiC an 'in-situ reinforcing phase' and the mechanism calls it an 'in-situ formed ceramic phase'; no reaction or precursor route that would form TiC in situ is specified.
